title: 7 Best PowerApps Alternatives in 2026 (Free, Open-Source and AI-Native)
summary: The 7 best PowerApps alternatives in 2026: Vybe, Retool, Airtable, AppSheet, Appsmith, Budibase and Glide, compared on AI building, licensing and who runs the app after you ship it.
body_markdown:
*PowerApps is still the first answer for a team inside Microsoft 365 that needs an internal app. It is also a platform whose licensing math got tighter in 2026: Microsoft closed the per-app plan to new customers, announced the first Premium price increase in more than five years and starts enforcing premium licensing in February 2027. This guide compares seven PowerApps alternatives, from free and open-source builders to AI-native platforms, and keeps one question in front: who runs the app after you ship it?*


## What is the best PowerApps alternative?


It depends on what you need. Here is the short version:


- Best overall if you want the app built and run for you: Vybe. An agent builds it from a description and keeps operating it after you ship, which no other option on this list does.
- Best for engineering teams: Retool, if your people live in SQL and JavaScript and want one of the deepest integration catalogs in the category.
- Best for structured business data: Airtable, when your process is really a database that needs an interface and automations around it.
- Best inside Google Workspace: AppSheet, with the tightest Sheets and Drive integration and offline mobile support.
- Best free and open-source option: Appsmith, Apache 2.0 licensed, self-hosted, with no per-user license at all.
- Best open-source option for operations teams: Budibase, whose agents became request-driven and approval-gated in version 4.0.
- Best for spreadsheet-to-app speed: Glide, which now ships as two products, including an AI agent platform called GlideOS.


If you want AI to build the tool *and* run it after you ship, that is Vybe. We also compare the wider low-code field, Retool included, in[Vybe vs. Retool vs. Lovable vs. Base44 vs. Superblocks](https://www.vybe.build/blog/vybe-vs-retool-vs-lovable-vs-base44-vs-superblocks) .


## Why teams replace PowerApps in 2026


Licensing is the first reason, and 2026 tightened it from three directions at once.


The low-cost middle path disappeared. The per-app plan, which licensed one app for one user, stopped being available to new customers through several purchasing channels on January 2, 2026, according to Microsoft's licensing overview. A pay-as-you-go meter remains for occasional users, but the predictable cheap option for a small department app is gone, and the remaining paths assume every active user carries a license.


The price went up. On September 9, 2026, Microsoft announced a per-user list price increase for Power Apps Premium, its first in more than five years, effective January 1, 2027 for new purchases and renewals. Existing subscriptions keep their price through their current term.


Enforcement is coming. Microsoft's licensing FAQ tells customers to prepare for licensing enforcement beginning in February 2027, which is when the gap between who built an app and who is licensed to run it stops being theoretical.


Even the free path narrowed. Unmanaged developer environments, the sandboxes a free Developer Plan used to create, can no longer be created as of November 15, 2026. Microsoft suspends existing ones on December 15, 2026 and starts deleting them on January 15, 2027. The managed environments that replace them are part of the paid licenses.


Under the licensing sit two runtime limits from Microsoft's own documentation. Delegation first: when a canvas app filter or lookup cannot be delegated to the data source, Power Apps processes the records locally, 500 rows by default and 2,000 at most even after you raise the setting. On a table with tens of thousands of rows, a non-delegable filter quietly returns partial results, and users stop trusting what the screen shows them. Then premium connectors: the connectors most business apps need, SQL Server, Salesforce or SAP, sit behind premium licensing. The use rights included with Microsoft 365 cover standard connectors and Microsoft data, and the transition window that let older apps run SQL-backed screens on Office-seeded licenses closed on October 1, 2024.


Add the learning curve: canvas apps, model-driven apps, Power Fx, Power Automate and Dataverse are five surfaces to master before a department ships anything serious.


And there is the quieter issue, the one that decides most renewals: in Power Apps you build the screen and you own the maintenance. Microsoft owns the runtime, the connector rules and the enforcement calendar. When the app breaks at 2am, someone on your side gets the call.

## Vybe: the AI-native option that runs the app for you


Vybe is the pick when you want the app owned, not just built. An agent builds it from a description, and after you publish, an agent keeps operating it against a goal it owns: a number, a budget and a scope. That is the difference between a task-based agent and a goal-based one, and it is the whole reason the product does not end at "here is your app." We covered that distinction in[AI App Builder vs. AI Agent Platform](https://www.vybe.build/blog/ai-app-builder-vs-ai-agent-platform) and, more directly, in[Agents are task-based. They should be goal-based.](https://www.vybe.build/blog/agents-are-task-based-they-should-be-goal-based)


I build on Vybe every day, so weigh what I say about it accordingly: we make Vybe. And the limits matter more than the pitch. Vybe is young. Its connector catalog is far smaller than Microsoft's more than 1,000 connectors, so deep SharePoint or Dynamics 365 work is not its ground. There is no offline mobile mode. If your data lives in Dataverse, migrating it is real work. If your app is a forms-and-approvals process glued to Microsoft 365 and no one complains, staying is a legitimate answer.


A free tier with 100 daily credits is enough to build a real workflow app and see whether an agent operating it changes how your team works.


## Retool: the engineer's alternative


Retool is the pick when the team is engineers and the tool needs to be precise. You write SQL and JavaScript directly, you wire your own databases and APIs in, and the 2026 changelog shows the AI investment is real: an app-building agent, Retool Agents speaking the A2A protocol since December 2025, and a generally available MCP server since November 11, 2026 that lets outside coding agents inspect and edit workflows. We cover Retool in depth in[8 Best Retool Alternatives in 2026](https://www.vybe.build/blog/best-retool-alternatives) .


What it does is give engineers speed without giving up control. What it does not own is anything after you ship. Someone on your team still runs the app, and the per-user model prices seats rather than occasional business users. If your PowerApps app broke because no one owned it, Retool hands that problem right back to you.


## Airtable: the database-first alternative


Airtable is the alternative when your PowerApps app was really a database wearing a form. Its Fall 2026 release, announced November 18, 2026, made that case stronger: Omni 2.0, the first-party agent, now builds data models, imports messy files and configures automations in one pass, and Airtable Canvas went generally available on every plan, building apps, dashboards and presentations from your live data in plain language. Agent audit logs record what agents did to your bases, and agent permissions are next on the roadmap.


Two things to weigh. AI work runs on bundled monthly credits that do not roll over, so a busy team needs to watch the meter. And ownership of the company changed: Bending Spoons completed its acquisition in early September 2026, and the product lead's October 2026 roadmap post commits to holding plans and prices for the coming months. Watch it, but nothing has changed for customers yet.


## Google AppSheet: the Workspace-native alternative


AppSheet is the closest experience to PowerApps if your world is Google rather than Microsoft. Apps build on Sheets and Drive data, forms and checklists run offline with background sync, and Gemini for App Creation, included in the paid licenses, proposes tables, columns and views from a plain-language description of your process.


One fact from Google itself deserves weight. On May 15, 2026, the AppSheet team published a product strategy update saying engineering is prioritizing stability and reliability, and that new feature development will be significantly reduced as a result. If you want a platform that keeps adding capability, AppSheet is telling you plainly to expect less of that for now. If what burned you was an app that kept breaking, the same update is their promise.


## Appsmith: the free open-source alternative


Appsmith is where the license disappears entirely. It is Apache 2.0 licensed, you self-host it and your users never see a per-seat subscription. The 2026 releases moved it toward the AI-native camp too: Ask AI came to the free Community Edition in version 2.3, and version 2.4 added an MCP server in beta, where an outside agent builds and edits apps through a structured tool API and confirms destructive operations with a human in the loop.


The trade is the classic open-source one. You own the hosting, the upgrades and the patching. The late-2026 release notes included several upgrade-breaking notes, among them a Java runtime fix that every self-hosted instance needed to apply. Budget an engineer for that work and the license savings stay real.


## Budibase: the open-source alternative for operations teams


Budibase 4.0, released on November 10, 2026, took its agents out of beta and rebuilt them around accountability. Each agent operation creates a persistent, trackable request. Approval policies decide what an agent may do on its own, and humans can approve from Slack or Teams. For an operations team that wants open source and a human in the loop by design, that is the draw.


As with Appsmith, self-hosting is free and the cloud is paid. Budibase fits CRUD apps and approval flows on top of a database you already run. If your PowerApps app grew into heavy business logic, test that part before you commit.


## Glide: the spreadsheet-to-app alternative


Glide rebuilt itself around an agent. Its newer product, GlideOS, is a separate platform from the original Glide Classic, and a September 1, 2026 changelog entry restructured its plans into Free, Basic, Plus, Pro and Enterprise tiers, with credits metering the agent's work. Data triggers shipped on October 19, 2026: a workflow starts the moment a row is added, updated or deleted, instead of waking on a schedule to check.


Glide is the fastest road from spreadsheet to working app, and that is exactly where a lot of PowerApps stories start. What sits outside its center of gravity is the enterprise layer, deep governance and legacy-system connectors, which is where the older products on this list are stronger.


## FAQ


### Is Power Apps free?


The Developer Plan is free for building and testing. Production is different: users who touch premium connectors or Dataverse-backed apps need a premium license, and Microsoft's licensing FAQ describes enforcement beginning in February 2027. The free plan's unmanaged developer environments also stopped being created on November 15, 2026.


### Can a Power Apps app use SQL Server without a premium license?


Mostly no. The transition window that let older apps run SQL-backed screens on Microsoft 365-seeded licenses closed on October 1, 2024, so premium connectors now require premium licensing for the users who run the app.


### What replaced the Power Apps per-app plan?


Nothing with the same shape. Microsoft stopped offering the per-app plan to new customers through several purchasing channels on January 2, 2026 and kept a pay-as-you-go meter that bills per active user per app each month. The predictable low-cost tier for a small department app is the part that went away.


## Which PowerApps alternative should you pick?


If your team is engineers, Retool. If your process is a database, Airtable. If you live in Google Workspace, AppSheet. If the license bill is the problem and you can host it, Appsmith or Budibase. If you want the fastest path from spreadsheet to app, Glide.


And if what pushed you out of Power Apps is that no one owns the app once it ships, that is the problem Vybe is built for. I would start smaller than a migration plan: build one real workflow on the free tier and watch what the agent does with it after you publish.[Try Vybe free](https://www.vybe.build/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=cta&utm_campaign=agents&utm_content=best-powerapps-alternatives) .
